newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia to buy 10 Russian helicopters.
newsitem.headline: Colombia to buy 10 Russian helicopters.

text.p: The Colombian military will buy 10 Russian-made Mi-17-IV helicopters to boost its fight against leftist rebels, the Defence Ministry said on Thursday.

The deal accounts for 40 percent of an agreed $107 million budget for buying a fleet of helicopters. The remainder will be spent on an unspecified number of U.S.-made Blackhawks and French-made Cougars, the ministry added.

U.S. President Bill Clinton three weeks ago announced a separate military aid package for Colombia that includes 32 UH-1H helicopters, five C-26 observation planes, all-terrain vehicles and riverboats.

"The Russian helicopters have the best internal load bearing capacity and have the lowest operating costs and are a good alternative for logistical and rearguard operations even if they may have limitations in terms of transporting troops into combat zones," Defence Minister Juan Carlos Esguerra said in a communique.
For the last six weeks, Colombia's security forces have been fighting to contain what military experts say is the bloodiest guerrilla offensive in more than three decades of armed uprising.

The army has been severely limited by its lack of airborne forward mobility. Reinforcements have to be moved in to remote jungle and mountain areas by land and river, exposing them to guerrilla ambushes and wasting vital hours.

The Russian helicopters will improve troop mobility but Esguerra accepted that their speed and manoeuvrability were inferior to the European and U.S. craft. Negotiations for the purchase of the Blackhawks and Cougars are expected to begin within a month.
Last month the United States announced a total of $112 million in military aid and training to Colombia, Venezuela, Mexico and the Caribbean.
Colombia will receive $40 million of that, with three-quarters going to the army and the remainder to the national police, which plays a lead role in the fight against drugs.
Colombia was decertified by the United States as an ally in the drug war in March for what U.S. officials said was President Ernesto Samper's failure to do enough to curb the scourge.

But efforts by Colombia to win back certification together with its success in convincing U.S. authorities of the link between drug trafficking and the country's leftist guerrillas is leading to closer anti-drug and counterinsurgency cooperation, political analysts say.
